## Why this chapter matters {#sec-ims-why}

The international monetary system is the set of rules — some written down, most not — that decides how currencies are valued against one another, how countries settle what they owe, and who supplies the money everyone else holds in reserve. Over the past 230 years the world has tried bimetallism, gold, managed pegs and floating rates. Each regime solved the problem left by the one before and created a new one of its own.

**Key questions**

- Why did gold win over silver in the nineteenth century, and why did it fail in the twentieth?
- What did Bretton Woods promise, and why could the United States not keep the promise?
- Why can no country have a fixed exchange rate, open capital markets and its own monetary policy all at once?
- Why does the dollar still sit at the centre of a system with no formal anchor?

## Two centuries in one picture {#sec-ims-timeline}

```{python}
#| label: d02-timeline
#| fig-cap: "**Exhibit 2.1** Two centuries of the international monetary system. Regime boundaries are conventional dates; transitions took years."
dx.ims_timeline(); plt.show()
```

**Bimetallism and the British exception.** The U.S. Coinage Act of 1792 defined the dollar in both gold and silver. Britain drifted onto gold instead, and resumed paying gold for its notes in 1821 after the Napoleonic Wars.

**The classical gold standard, 1870s–1914.** Once Germany switched to gold after 1871 and the United States resumed convertibility in 1879, the major currencies were fixed to each other through gold: one pound bought \$4.8665. Capital moved freely, and London sat at the centre.

**Interwar disorder.** Gold was suspended in 1914. Britain returned in 1925 at the prewar parity, which overvalued the pound, and was forced off again in 1931. The United States devalued to \$35 an ounce in 1934, and the decade dissolved into devaluations and controls.

**Bretton Woods, 1944–1973.** Currencies were pegged to the dollar, and the dollar to gold at \$35. Capital controls made the pegs workable. As dollars piled up abroad, the gold promise became impossible to keep; on 15 August 1971 Nixon closed the gold window, and by 1973 the major currencies floated.

**The floating-dollar era.** Today the major currencies float, many others still peg, twenty-one European countries share the euro, and the dollar still makes up **`{python} f"{float(val('cofer_usd')):.1f}"` percent** of the world's identified foreign-exchange reserves.

```{python}
#| label: d02-gbp
#| fig-cap: "**Exhibit 2.2** The pound in dollars. Under gold and Bretton Woods the rate was a policy decision that changed in steps; since 1971 it has been a market price that changes every second."
dx.gbp_dollar(); plt.show()
```

## The impossible trinity {#sec-ims-trilemma}

```{python}
#| label: d02-trilemma
#| fig-cap: "**Exhibit 2.3** The impossible trinity. The gold standard chose fixed rates and free capital; Bretton Woods chose fixed rates and monetary independence; the floating era chose free capital and independence."
dx.trilemma(); plt.show()
```

**Running case.** Chattanooga Precision Components' Mexican subsidiary would have faced a peso fixed at 12.50 to the dollar from 1954 to 1976. Today the same subsidiary's dollar value moves daily — a direct consequence of the corner Mexico now occupies in Exhibit 2.3.

## The Ascent of Money · Niall Ferguson (book, 2008; PBS series)
**Watch or read:** Chapter 2, "Of Human Bondage", tells how Nathan Rothschild gathered gold across Europe to pay Wellington's armies before Waterloo in 1815, and how the bond market made his family the most powerful financiers of the gold-standard century. Chapter 6, "From Empire to Chimerica", follows the first age of globalization to its collapse in 1914 and asks whether the U.S.–China financial relationship could end the same way.

**What it gets wrong:** Ferguson tells the story through memorable financiers. The regime changes in Exhibit 2.1 owed at least as much to politics and to the arithmetic of Exhibit 2.3.
:::
